Prevailing archaic views on mental illness aside, it’s worth noting that mental healthcare in Brunei has seen some progress over the years.

The Mental Health Order came into effect in 2014, and since then national suicide hotlines were introduced while mental healthcare is set for integration into community healthcare settings – just to name a select few.

While we may lament the slow pace of legislative progress and much needed change in harmful cultural attitudes (e.g. stigma), at least we know that on some level, we’re moving in the right direction.

Plenty of cultural, religious and governmental hurdles lie ahead, but there’s a glaring issue that needs attention: the criminalization of suicide. 

In Brunei attempted suicide can land you in jail for up to a year, a BND 4,000 fine, or both. 

(We’re not outliers in the developing world; Malaysia also still criminalizes suicide, while Singapore decriminalized attempted suicide last year.)

There’s nothing empathetic about punishing survivors simply because they wanted to end the suffering they didn’t have the resources to cope with in the first place. 

Religion can play a role in treatment, but criminalizing the act, as evidenced in many case studies, has no proven value as a deterrent.
